bio.en: Jessica Lachs is Vice President of Analytics and Data Science at DoorDash, where she has built one of the largest and most respected data teams in tech over a 10+-year tenure and was the company's first GM launching new markets; she previously founded the social-gifting startup GiftSimple.
bio.zh: Jessica Lachs 是 DoorDash 的分析与数据科学副总裁，在十余年任期里打造了科技圈规模最大、最受尊敬的数据团队之一，也是公司开拓新市场的第一位 GM；她此前创办了社交送礼初创 GiftSimple。

summary.en: Jessica makes the case that analytics should be a business-impact function, not a service desk—answering 'what do we do now?' not just 'why?'. She argues for a centralized data org, explains why retention is a terrible metric to goal on (find a short-term measure that drives long-term output), and shares what to look for when hiring data people. The conversation is full of concrete examples of how DoorDash's data team shaped real decisions, plus great stories from the company's scrappy early days.
summary.zh: Jessica 主张分析应当是一个“驱动业务影响”的职能，而非服务台——回答“我们现在该怎么做？”，而不只是“为什么？”。她主张数据团队集中化，解释了为何“留存”是个糟糕的考核指标（应找一个能驱动长期产出的短期指标），并分享了招聘数据人才时看重的点。对话充满了 DoorDash 数据团队如何影响真实决策的具体案例，以及公司草创期的精彩故事。

turns.en: Retention is a terrible thing to goal on. It's almost impossible to drive in a meaningful way in a short term. Ultimately, you want to find a short-term metric you can measure that drives a long-term output.

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: There's two main things that I think are important when you're structuring a team. The first is I believe that analytics should have a seat at the table just like engineering and product and the business folks, the operators. For me, analytics is a business impact driving function and not purely a service function. I think there are analytics teams at other companies where they are answering people's questions, maybe even through Jira tickets, we're building dashboards. That was never really of interest to me. That wasn't the team that I wanted to build. (00:05:35): For me, it's about finding opportunities, about having a point of view on the decisions that we should make, not just answering the why but answering the so what. "So what do we do now that we know this?" And so that's definitely one thing as far as my point of view on building a data team. I think the second thing which may be a little more contrarian is I think there are people out there who think that analytics should be embedded into business units. I strongly disagree. I believe a central model, a center of excellence is superior and I'm happy to talk about why, but that's something that I feel quite strongly about. We've tried it or I shouldn't... well, we've experimented in the past with the alternative, so putting it into a business unit and it's just much more problematic and I think the value you get from a central model is far greater than some of the things that you might lose.
turns.zh:
关于如何组建团队，我认为有两点至关重要。首先，我认为分析团队应当与工程、产品及业务部门（包括运营人员）同等重要地参与决策过程。对我而言，分析团队应当作为推动业务成果的职能部门，而非单纯的服务型部门。我曾在其他公司见过这样的分析团队，他们只是被动地解答问题，或许甚至通过Jira工单处理用户需求，但这类团队并不能真正激发我的兴趣——这不是我想要打造的团队。

（00:05:35）对我而言，关键在于寻找机遇，为我们应当做出的决策提供见解。不仅要回答“为什么要做”，也要思考“现在该怎么做”。当我们掌握了这些信息后，下一步该如何行动？这就是我构建数据团队的核心理念。

第二点观点可能更具争议性——我认为分析团队不应嵌入业务部门。我坚决反对这种做法。我坚信集中式模式（即卓越中心）更胜一筹，具体原因我乐意展开探讨。但我们曾尝试过将分析团队嵌入业务部门的做法，结果却问题重重。与集中式模式相比，嵌入式模式的价值实在微不足道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, let's definitely talk about it. And just to make sure people understand, when you say central versus embedded, is that in terms of reporting lines, in terms of their goals?
turns.zh: 好的，我们确实需要深入探讨这个问题。首先，您提到的“集中式”和“嵌入式”模式，是指汇报线还是团队目标呢？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: It's a great question. So mostly it's in terms of reporting lines because I think on the goal side, that is something where we have the same goals that our partner teams have, and I think that that's actually an important part of a successful central model. So when I say central model, it just means that for marketing analytics, marketing analytics is part of the broader analytics team. It does not sit and report in through marketing. Just to clarify.
turns.zh: 这个问题问得很好。主要体现在汇报线层面，因为我认为在目标设定上，我们与合作团队的目标是一致的，这正是集中式模式成功的关键所在。所以我所说的集中式模式，指的是市场分析团队作为更广泛的分析团队的一部分，而非单独向市场部门汇报。这里需要明确一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So the reporting functions at some companies, there's the head of marketing or some partners to the head of marketing where the data, say, analyst or biz ops people or data scientists would report potentially to them and that's it. And they're not as connected to the core, to the rest of the data team, the rest of the analytics team versus-
turns.zh: 明白了。有些公司的汇报机制是，市场部负责人或其上级直接接收数据分析师、业务运营人员或数据科学家的汇报，仅此而已。他们与核心数据团队或分析团队的联系并不紧密——

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Exactly. Yeah.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: So you'd have a bunch of smaller, of course, data teams that sit embedded within the functions. And I understand why business leaders like that. You're embedded within the function, so you're a part of the team. That ownership, that camaraderie that comes with that, I think you can solve for that. But I do understand that that is a benefit. I think the other benefit of course is the business leaders control the roadmaps so they get to dictate the work. They know that they have help and resources in that area when they need them. So that certainty, that control, I totally understand the value there, but I think that those are two things that you can solve for if you know that those are the biggest issues with a central team. So for us, we have a central analytics team, but we are divided up into pods that map perfectly with how product engineering, operations marketing are structured as well. (00:08:33): And so our team de facto has these folks embedded with our partner teams, even though the reporting structure is up through a central org through me. And that helps the team to feel like they are one team, both in terms of the analytics team feeling like it's one team, but also to use the marketing example, the marketing folks are one team and because the analytics shares the same goals as the marketing leaders, your incentives are aligned to work on the most important things and your success is their success and vice versa. So I think that that's been really a happy medium, but still preserves all the benefits of a central org. And there are a lot of them.
turns.zh:
因此，你会有许多规模较小的数据团队，嵌入在各个职能部门中。我理解为什么企业领导者喜欢这种模式。你嵌入在职能部门中，因此成为团队的一员。这种归属感和团队协作精神，我认为是可以解决的。但我确实理解这种模式的优势。另一个好处当然是，业务领导者可以掌控项目路线图，从而主导工作进程。当他们需要数据支持时，知道能获得所需的帮助和资源。因此，这种确定性和掌控权的优势，我完全理解其价值。但我认为，如果你知道这是中央团队面临的最大挑战，那么这些问题都是可以解决的。

对我们来说，我们有一个中央分析团队，但我们被分成多个小组，这些小组与产品工程、运营和营销等部门的结构完美匹配。（00:08:33）：因此，我们的团队实际上将这些人员嵌入到合作伙伴团队中，尽管汇报层级是通过中央组织向我汇报的。这有助于团队感觉自己是一个整体——无论是分析团队，还是以营销为例，营销团队都是一个整体。由于分析团队与营销领导者有着相同的目标，双方的激励机制一致，致力于解决最重要的问题，彼此的成功也相互促进。因此，我认为这是一个很好的折中方案，同时也保留了中央组织的所有优势。这样的例子还有很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to hear about them, but I think something that some people may think when you say essential org is like a silo data team that sits there and they're like a service org a little bit within the company. It's like, "Hey, I need some data help." And you try to convince that, "Hey, I need some help on this thing." And that's not what you're saying.
turns.zh: 我想听听你的具体做法，但有些人可能会认为“核心组织”就像一个独立的数据团队，坐在那里充当公司内部的服务部门。就像，“嘿，我需要数据方面的帮助。”然后你试图说服他们，“嘿，我需要你帮忙解决这个问题。”但这不是你的意思。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Oh, no. No, no, no. That job seems terrible. I don't want that job. No, to the earlier point, we have a seat at the table. We are business partners, we are thought partners with our product counterparts, with our engineering counterparts, with our ops counterparts, and we again, share the same goals and have the same initiatives that they do. And it's just our job to come at it from a data-driven place. We bring to the table insights on things that we've noticed, deep dives that we do to understand the problems that we're trying to solve better. If we need to grow, what are the most efficient ways to grow? What are the trade-offs that we have to make? Where are their pockets of opportunity? That is what I expect my team to be able to bring to that table, the proverbial table, that we want to see that. And in order to earn their spot, that's the deal. We get the seat at the table and we need to earn it by bringing opportunities that we all can go and go after.
turns.zh: 哦，不，不，不，不。那种工作听起来很糟糕。我可不想做那种工作。不，回到前面提到的观点，我们在决策桌上有一席之地。我们是业务伙伴，是与产品团队、工程团队、运营团队的思想伙伴。我们与他们共享相同的目标和倡议。我们的工作就是从数据驱动的角度看问题。我们为他们提供见解，深入挖掘以更好地理解我们试图解决的问题。如果我们需要增长，最有效的增长方式是什么？我们需要做出哪些权衡？他们哪里有机会之窗？这就是我期望我的团队能在决策桌上（也就是所谓的‘谈判桌’）上展现出来的。而要赢得这个席位，这就是交易条件。我们在决策桌上占据一席之地，就必须通过提供大家都能追随的机会来证明自己的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So in a sense, it is embedded. They're embedded in cross-functional teams across the org, but they report up to essential org to you essentially in the end?
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以从某种意义上说，他们是嵌入式的。他们嵌入在整个组织的跨职能团队中，但最终向你汇报到中央组织吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. What are some of the benefits of this approach?
turns.zh: 不错。这种方法有哪些好处？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Oh, there's so many. Okay, so the first thing is a consistent and high talent bar. I think this is something I saw when we would have some pockets of analytics folks embedded is having a consistent bar for talent in terms of what we're looking for, what are the technical skills, what are the soft skills? And being able to evaluate candidates with that same bar, using our same rubric. You just get more consistent and higher talent in my opinion. I think that's number one. Number two is actually growth opportunities. So if you're siloed, you may be the most senior data person within... I keep picking on marketing. But you might be the most senior data scientist within marketing. Where do you go from there? I think when you have the central org, you're able to see if there are growth opportunities in other areas within the company. (00:12:04): And so that really helps folks to stay engaged because they can look at new problems if the problems they've been working on for several years are getting maybe boring and they want something new, there's an opportunity, move from marketing over to merchant analytics. And then I think similarly, if there isn't a promotion or room to grow, if you want to be a people manager and there just isn't a people management role within your functional area, well, you've got 10 other ones to look at and maybe there is that opportunity. So I think it helps with the growth opportunities for the team, which helps to retain talent. So that's a second thing. The third thing is just consistency of methodologies and metrics. So you don't have sales that was as defined by one team and sales as defined by another team. You just have sales and everybody is using the same metrics, the same methodologies, and you're able to improve your methodologies with input from more people. (00:13:10): And rather than recreating the wheel, building the same churn prediction model on six different teams. You can instead build one and have the input of six different teams. I think that's definitely another benefit. Also helps you just scale because you start to see the same problems across teams and so you're like, "Ooh, this is an issue that we need to get ahead of. This is something we need to automate," or, "This is something that we need to improve upon," or, "a problem that is going to grow as our business, as our teams scales." So I think it helps you see around corners a little bit more. (00:13:45): And then just lastly, there's a team culture brand. I think that's really important, not just externally for recruiting top talent, but the team is really proud to be members of the analytics team. We have a unique culture of learning, of sharing. You have someone you can go to talk about your challenges. You have someone who can peer review your work. I think just having that team culture that we have is really important. And it's a lot harder to get when you have the individual silos, particularly in an earlier stage when it's a smaller team, you just don't have as many people around. Everybody wants to have friends at work and we're creating an environment where they can find like-minded data nerds.
turns.zh:
天哪，太多要点了。好的，首先是保持一致且高标准的人才筛选机制。我认为这是在我们嵌入分析团队时，看到的一个关键点——即在人才标准、技术技能和软技能方面要设定统一的衡量标准。用同样的评分标准去评估候选人，最终能招到更稳定、更高素质的人才。这是我认为最重要的一点。

第二点是成长机会。如果你被困在孤立的部门，比如我在营销部门的例子——你可能是营销团队中最资深的数据科学家。但接下来该怎么发展呢？当有中央团队时，就能看到公司其他部门的成长机会。（00:12:04）这能帮助员工保持积极性，因为当他们深耕多年的项目变得枯燥时，可以转向新领域。比如从营销转到商家分析。同样，如果没有晋升机会或发展空间，比如想成为人力经理但所在部门没有相关职位，那其他部门总有空缺。这能为团队创造成长机会，进而留住人才。

第三点是方法论和指标的统一。比如不要让不同团队对销售数据有不同定义。统一使用相同的指标和方法论，还能集思广益改进流程。（00:13:10）而不是让六个团队各自开发相同的客户流失预测模型，而是整合六个团队的智慧。这无疑是另一个优势。它还能助力规模化——当团队发现相似问题时，就能提前预警、自动化或改进流程，避免重复造轮子。

最后是团队文化品牌。这不仅对外招揽顶尖人才很重要，更重要的是团队成员对数据分析团队的自豪感。我们拥有独特的学习与分享文化，有人能倾听你的挑战，也有人会审阅你的工作。这种文化氛围在分散的团队中很难形成，尤其在初期规模较小的团队中，团队成员更需要这样的归属感。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It makes me think about Airbnb's first data team. I don't know if you know Riley Newman well, but he built Airbnb's first data team and it was actually an analytics team. They called themselves the 'A-Team' on the point of culture, and that always felt a lot of fun and they loved being part of that team.
turns.zh: 这让我想起Airbnb的首个数据团队。我不知道你是否了解莱利·纽曼，但他组建的Airbnb首个数据团队其实就是一个分析团队。他们以"A-Team"为名，强调团队文化，总是充满乐趣，成员们都乐于成为其中一员。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah. We have the same, but now I feel a lot less special for coming up with that name.
turns.zh: 是啊。我们也有过类似的经历，但现在一想到自己想出那个名字就觉得自己没那么了不起了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, you called it A-Team also?
turns.zh: 哦，你也把它叫做A-Team吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, we got the A-Team, yeah.
turns.zh: 对啊，我们当时用的就是A-Team。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then I think they moved away from it when there was a push. Now we're data scientists, we're not analytics or analysts. And that was like, I don't know, 10 year ago, like [inaudible 00:15:08] data science. We're data scientists.
turns.zh: 后来当有新的业务需求时，我们就放弃了这个名字。现在我们是数据科学家，不再是分析师或分析员了。那都是大约10年前的事了，当时（听不清00:15:08）数据科学还处于起步阶段。我们现在就是数据科学家。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: We'll always be the A-Team.
turns.zh: 我们永远都是A-Team。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many threads I want to follow here, one that's a tangent, but something that I think a lot of people struggle with is you talked about how you want your data team, your analytics team to be proactive, to find opportunities, to give you ideas, to help you figure out what to build, not just answer questions. At the same time, there are many questions that teams need to get answered. Do you have any advice for just how to set up a team where they both find time to explore, dig, show opportunities and come up with big ideas and also, "Hey, we just need to figure out the funnel conversion on this thing," or "Hey, what do you think? What's happening in China right now?" Thoughts there?
turns.zh: 这里有太多我想深入探讨的点了。其中一个偏题的话题是，很多人都面临的挑战是，你提到希望数据团队、分析团队能够主动出击，寻找机会，为你提供思路，帮助你确定要开发的项目，而不只是回答问题。与此同时，团队也需要处理很多日常问题。你有没有什么建议，能让团队既有时间探索、挖掘、发现机会，又能产出像“我们需要优化这个转化漏斗”或者“你怎么看？中国现在的情况如何？”这样的实用见解？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, such a good question. I think it's something that never gets easier. You have to be very intentional to carve out time for exploratory work for deep dives because as you mentioned, there are always more questions and more work to be done than hours in the day. And so I think being intentional about it and setting goals for your team around finding these insights through self-directed work is an important mechanism for holding ourselves accountable to that goal because it tends to be the first thing that goes when you get a lot of inbounds, you're like, "All right, well, let's deep dive on something that I don't know if it's really something. It could be high ROI, it could be low ROI, I don't know." So the expected value is lower than this known thing that I can deliver and make someone happy. (00:16:42): So I think to prevent that time from just slipping away, you really have to be intentional. We would do hackathons for our team to carve out days to just go and look into these really interesting things and find opportunities. And I think we have the support of our business partners because so many great insights have come from these deep dives and it really has been some of the work that drives future roadmaps. So they're always really great at allowing us to have this time and actually encourage us often to have this time for some self-directed work, to go find the next big opportunity.
turns.zh: 嗯，这确实是个难题。必须刻意为探索性工作和深度研究腾出时间，因为正如你所说，每天要处理的问题和工作量永远超出可用时间。所以我觉得，团队要刻意为此设定目标，通过自主学习来挖掘这些洞察，这对自我约束至关重要。因为当大量突发任务涌来时，人们往往会先放下这些探索性的工作，因为不确定它是否真的有价值，可能高ROI，也可能低ROI，难以预料。所以预期价值远低于那些已知的、能让别人满意的成果。（00:16:42）所以要防止这些时间被白白浪费，就必须有意识地安排。我们会为团队举办黑客马拉松，专门腾出几天时间，让大家去研究那些真正感兴趣的领域，寻找机会。我们得到了业务伙伴的大力支持，因为很多重大洞察都来自这些深度研究，也确实为未来的路线图提供了方向。所以他们总是很支持我们腾出时间，让我们自由探索，寻找下一个重大机遇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If there's no answer that comes to mind, that's totally cool. But is there an example of one of these insights that someone on the data team came up with that led to something big for DoorDash that you're able to share?
turns.zh: 如果现在暂时想不出例子，那也没关系。但有没有数据团队成员提出的某个洞察，最终为DoorDash带来了重大成果，你能分享一下？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: So one interesting example was from a hackathon we did a couple of years ago where we were looking at referral as a channel for consumer acquisition. And when you compare that channel to others, it was below average in terms of the engagement you'd see from consumers who came through that channel and the payback period. And rather than just lowering spend on referrals and moving right along, we really wanted to understand what was happening. And so during the hackathon, we did a deep dive into referral. We actually tried referring each other. We tried committing referral fraud, creating new accounts to get around rules. And we uncovered a lot of fraudulent behavior through this deep dive. We ordered so many cupcakes to the office. I remember using referral credits because you had to place an order to be able to get the referral bonus. So we would create the account, place the orders, and we just kept ordering cupcakes. (00:18:39): And what we noticed was that referral as a channel was a bit misleading when you would look at the average in terms of payback and that it was really a bimodal distribution and you had one group of really great consumers who were referring other really great consumers, and the payback on those consumers was really strong. In fact, if that's all you saw, you would spend a lot more on that channel. (00:19:08): And then what was happening was you had this other group of consumers that were not as good people who were posting referral codes online and getting people who were just in it to get free discounts and credits. And we had at that point in time, pretty lax fraud rules. And we didn't have caps on these things. All of which came about from this deep dive where we found that this group of consumers was really a drag on the efficiency of this marketing channel. And so I think that's an example of a few things that we like to do at DoorDash. One being these deep dives and taking the time to really understand the problem and then ultimately make a bunch of recommendations for what we should do, including better fraud checks, caps on referrals, et cetera, et cetera. But also how the average can be incredibly misleading. And so looking at distributions and trying to break down what you're seeing to find ways that you can optimize in ways that you can gain in efficiencies.
turns.zh: 举个有趣的例子，是我们几年前参加的一次黑客马拉松，当时我们把引荐作为用户获取的渠道来研究。当把这个渠道与其他渠道相比时，它在用户参与度和回报周期方面都表现平平。我们没有简单地削减引荐推广的预算，而是深入剖析了其中的问题。黑客马拉松期间，我们对引荐机制进行了深入研究，甚至互相互相推荐用户，尝试利用漏洞创建新账户获取奖励。通过这次深入调查，我们发现了大量欺诈行为。比如，我们曾大量订购纸杯蛋糕——因为引荐奖励需要下单才能领取，所以我们创建账户、下单，再不断重复这个过程。（00:18:39）我们发现，引荐作为获客渠道存在误导性——平均回报率存在双峰分布：一部分优质用户会推荐其他优质用户，回报率极高；另一部分用户则通过在网上发布引荐码吸引只为获取免费折扣和积分的用户。当时我们对欺诈行为管控宽松，没有设置上限。通过这次深入调查，我们发现这部分用户严重拖累了营销渠道效率。这也启发了我们在DoorDash的实践：一是深入研究问题，制定优化方案；二是揭示平均值的误导性，解析数据分布，优化策略效率。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome story, great memory to come up with that one. So this is a really good example of a way to carve out time for the data team to think long-term, think look for opportunities, find big ideas. So the hackathon is one idea. Imagine many data people are struggling often to push back on asks that are just like, "h, we need to know. We just need this one thing. Here's a question, just answer this one question part." Do you have any advice to data to get better at pushing back? Sounds like a bit of cultural like, "We have time, we need to work on these bigger things." But just any advice for data leaders or data ICs to find time for these sorts of things?
turns.zh: 这真是个精彩的故事，回忆起来很棒。这是为数据团队腾出时间进行长期思考、寻找机会、发现大创意的绝佳范例。黑客马拉松就是一个典型例子。想想看，很多数据人员经常被迫应付诸如“我们需要知道这个数据”、“回答这个问题”等被动请求。您对数据人员在抵制这种被动需求方面有什么建议吗？听起来需要一种文化转变：“我们有时间了，应该专注于更重要的事。”对于数据领导者或数据部门，如何为这类工作争取时间呢？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, saying no to someone is never fun. I think as a self-proclaimed people-pleaser, you don't want to say no, especially when it's something you can do and you know that you can very easily with maybe an hour's work, make someone happy. I think it's really important to establish a culture and for leadership to really establish the rules of working and that operating model so that some of the junior folks aren't forced to always have to say no. And I think one of the ways we do that is through our goaling. So because our goals are the same as our business partners, we're able to pretty easily say, "Hey, we've got a limited amount of time. These are our goals. What are the most important things that we are going to work on this week or this month in order for both of us to hit our goals?" (00:21:49): And so when something comes up to be able to say, "Hey, this data poll that you want me to do, is this more important than these other three things that I was going to be working on? Yes or no?" And I think sometimes people don't necessarily realize the trade-offs, and when you make them apparent and you put them front and center, they realize that, "Oh, actually, you know what? That asset's not important. That can wait." So I think that that's definitely something I would recommend, which is always share the trade-offs. Don't suffer in silence with, "How am I going to do all four of these things?" Bring it up and say, "Hey, this is what I was planning to do. If you want me to do this extra new thing, then one of these other things is going to have to drop. (00:22:36): I personally don't think that your ask is more important than these three things, but maybe there's new information, maybe there's context I don't have, so let's talk about it." Rather than just being like, "No, I won't do that." That's not a great approach either. I think having the conversation and constantly reevaluating your prioritization to make sure you're working on the most important things or your team is working on the most important things is really good hygiene to have with your business partner. So some teams do that through a weekly standup like, "Here's what we're going to do this week. Do we like this prioritization? Do we not?" Some folks do it less formally than that. I think you got to figure out what works for you. But to the earlier point, it's a conversation with your engineering partner, your product partner, your ops partner, you're all on the same team, you're all trying to achieve the same goals and you're all incentivized to have your analytics team working on the most impactful things.
turns.zh: 是啊，对别人说不总是件容易的事。我觉得作为一个自认的讨好型人格，你总不愿意拒绝别人，尤其是当你明明能做到这件事时，只要花一个小时左右就能让别人开心。我认为建立一种文化非常重要，领导层也需要明确制定工作规则和运营模式，这样基层员工就不必总是被迫拒绝别人。我们通过设定目标来做到这一点，因为我们的目标与业务伙伴一致，所以我们能很轻松地说：“嘿，我们时间有限。这些是我们的目标。本周或本月我们要重点做哪几件事才能达成目标？”（00:21:49）当有新任务出现时，比如你想让我做这个数据调查，但它比我原本要做的其他三件事更重要吗？是或否？我觉得有时候人们不一定能意识到这种权衡。当你把这些权衡摆在明面上，他们就会意识到：“哦，实际上这项资产并不重要。它可以等一等。”所以我认为一定要分享这些权衡，而不是默默忍受。“我该怎么把这四件事都做完？”把问题提出来说：“嘿，我原本计划做这些事。如果你想让我做这项额外的新任务，那其他三项中的某一项就得往后排。”（00:22:36）我个人不认为你的请求比这三件事更重要，但也许有新信息，或许我还不知道上下文，所以我们来讨论一下。”而不是直接说“不，我不做”。这也不是个好办法。我认为和你的业务伙伴进行对话，持续重新评估优先级，确保你或你的团队都在做最重要的事，这才是和业务伙伴保持良好关系的关键。有些团队通过每周站会来做到这一点，比如“本周我们要做这些事。你们觉得这个优先级合理吗？不合理吗？”有些团队则不那么正式。但你得找到适合自己的方式。回到前面提到的观点，这就是和你的工程伙伴、产品伙伴、运维伙伴的对话。你们同属一个团队，都在为同一个目标而努力，都希望分析团队能专注于最有影响力的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This advice is great for any role basically. And if I were to summarize it to a couple words, it's just prioritize and communicate what your priorities are and then align on the trade-offs of shifting your priorities.
turns.zh: 这条建议对任何角色来说都非常实用。如果要用几个词概括，那就是优先排序并沟通你的优先事项，然后就调整优先事项的权衡达成一致。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Every once in a while you just throw one over and say, "You know what? This is quick. I'll do it." At least I do. I think sometimes just knock it out, build some goodwill. I think that that's also important. But usually it's not something you can do in five minutes and in that case it's that ruthless prioritization for sure.
turns.zh: 偶尔你会顺手接下：“你知道吗？这很快就能做完。我来做吧。”至少我会这样做。我觉得有时候直接做完，建立好感也很重要。但通常这不是五分钟就能完成的事，这种情况下当然需要严格的优先排序。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then there's also the side that you talked about of just show that you can provide value doing these things that are longer term, like prove your worth. "Hey, look at all these opportunities I found for our team over time, I should keep spending time on these other areas," versus the on fire stuff.
turns.zh: 然后还有你提到的另一面——你需要证明自己能通过做一些长期工作来创造价值，比如证明自己的价值。“嘿，看看我为团队找到的这些机会，我应该继续在其他领域投入时间。”而不是一味追求短期热点。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you're hiring people for your team, I'm curious what you look for and you think is incredibly important that maybe other people aren't prioritizing as much. What do you focus on when you're hiring?
turns.zh: 在为团队招聘人才时，我很好奇你会看重哪些特质，又认为哪些特质至关重要，而其他人可能不那么重视。招聘时你会重点关注什么？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah. So everybody needs to have a certain set of technical skills. I think that's a non-starter. We have a technical bar, we do a technical screen. So I think that's table stakes. There's some really unique characteristics that I've noticed when I look at some of the top talent that I've had on the team or have on the team. I think the first thing is just curiosity. You can't teach curiosity, or at least I haven't found a way to do it. If somebody else knows how, please let me know. Somebody who is just self-motivated to pull on the threads when they find them. So they don't just answer a question. They're like, "Hmm, this thing seems a little odd. I'm going to dig in and look. Even though I could say I'm done, I answered the question, I did the thing I was going to do." The person that has that curiosity, something seems off, something doesn't really make sense and goes and proactively looks into what that is. That is just so valuable. So I really look for that curiosity and that self-motivation to do it without being told.
turns.zh: 是的。每个人都需要具备一定的技术技能。我觉得这是一个基本要求。我们设定了技术门槛，也会进行技术筛选。所以我认为这属于入门标准。我注意到一些顶尖人才身上有一些非常独特的特质。首先就是好奇心。好奇心是无法教会的，至少我还没找到方法。如果有人知道方法，请告诉我。还有那些能主动挖掘问题的人。他们不只是回答问题，而是会说：“嗯，这个情况有点奇怪。我要深入调查一下。即使我已经完成了任务，回答了问题，也要继续挖掘。”那些有好奇心、能主动挖掘问题的人非常宝贵。所以我特别看重这种好奇心和主动性，不需要别人督促就能行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you test for that? How do you do that in an interview and get a sense of if they're good at that?
turns.zh: 如何测试这些特质？在面试中如何判断他们是否具备这些能力？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: One way you can do it through the questions you ask is have something that is not quite right within the case that you're presenting and see if people notice first and foremost. And even if they don't, if you point it out like, "Where do they go with that?" I think that that's something that you can test for. I think you can also ask for examples that for these folks typically will highlight this, they'll talk about, "I noticed this thing, and so we decided to investigate." So I think that there are ways that you can get that signal through the interview process, but it's really hard. I think testing for hard skills is a lot easier than testing for soft skills. And I think in some of the questions we ask, we'll ask a question with the idea that we're assessing something separate than what the question is necessarily asking. And I think that this is one example of where that really works.
turns.zh: 一种方法是通过提问来测试。比如在你给出的案例中故意设置一些不合理的地方，看看他们能否首先发现问题。即使他们没发现，你也可以指出问题并追问：“接下来你会怎么做？”我觉得这是一种测试方法。你也可以让他们举例说明，通常他们会说：“我注意到这个问题，于是我们决定深入调查。”所以在面试过程中确实有办法捕捉到这些信号，但这很难。我觉得测试硬技能比测试软技能容易得多。在某些问题中，我们会故意设置隐藏的考查点，比如通过一个问题来评估与问题本身无关的能力。这个例子就说明这种方法很有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said that you give them a case. What does that look like? What is the actual approach to how you do this interview?
turns.zh: 你说你会给他们一个案例。具体形式是怎样的？你如何进行这种面试？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Our interview process has in the early stages a coding exercise. So we do our technical screen and a shortened version of a business case. So real world problem solving. Typically, it's something actually from DoorDash history, like a real problem that we had to see how people can problem solve on the fly. I think that that's an important skill to be able to have, which is, how do you take a problem, break it down, talk through it. A little bit like some of those consulting cases that you hear about, but something that's really rooted in real problems. And I think you can learn a lot from those types of cases where, yes, you get to see how people handle ambiguity and structured problem solving, but ultimately most people get something wrong. They make an assumption that's wrong because well, I would hope that the interviewer knows the business better than the interviewee. (00:27:56): And seeing how people react to being told they're wrong is a really important signal in my opinion. Seeing how people respond, how they're able to take new information and pivot, how they're able to make a decision. So that's another thing that I like to see in cases where, hey, you may not know the real right decision. You might say, "Hey, I could see it going one way, I could see it going the other way." But I always push people to say, "If you had to make a call right now, what would it be?" So are people able to have a point of view without full information because that's life. Sometimes you have to just pick a direction and make a decision even though you don't have perfect information. So I like to see some of these softer skills and how they manifest throughout a case interview, even if it's not specifically what I'm asking with the literal problem we're solving in the case.
turns.zh: 我们的面试流程在初期会安排编程测试。因此，我们会进行技术筛选，并简化版的商业案例分析。这实际上是在解决现实世界中的问题。通常，这些案例会选自DoorDash的历史案例，旨在考察候选人如何即兴解决问题。这种能力至关重要——它需要你能将问题拆解、理清思路。这有点像你听说的那些咨询案例，但这些案例更贴近真实的商业场景。我认为从这类案例中能收获诸多启发。当然，你能看到人们如何应对不确定性，如何进行结构化问题解决，但最终多数人都会出错。他们会因为假设错误而误入歧途——毕竟，我希望面试官比应聘者更熟悉业务。（00:27:56）在我看来，观察应聘者面对错误时的反应至关重要。观察他们如何接受新信息、调整思路并做出决策。这也是我喜欢在面试中观察的另一项能力——当你无法确定最佳决策时，应聘者可能会说：“我觉得有两种可能的方向。”但我总会追问：“如果现在必须做出决定，你会怎么选？”这样能考察应聘者在信息不完备的情况下形成观点的能力，因为这就是现实。很多时候，你必须在不掌握完美信息的情况下做出选择。因此，我希望在案例面试中看到这些软技能的体现，即便这些技能与我们所解析的具体案例无关。

I don't exactly know the question, but I guess is there anything there that you think would be interesting for people to know or hear?
turns.zh: 再说回正题，但换个角度。您在投身这份工作前并没有深厚的数据科学背景。我知道您有艺术背景，学生时代有艺术作品集，我想很多人都难以想象像DoorDash这样的公司，分析部门的负责人竟有艺术背景。我不确定具体问题是什么，但您觉得有没有什么背景信息值得分享或探讨？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, it's funny. I joke that I have a job I'd never be hired for because I don't have a traditional data science background. And I know that Elizabeth Stone on her podcast with you talked a lot about her non-traditional background for a CTO. So hey, maybe there's something to it. But I became a data scientist out of necessity. I completely self-taught in terms of SQL and Python and I did it because there was a need at DoorDash for someone to help figure out what the right goals were, how we set those goals, how we were performing different markets early in the DoorDash story, so 10 years ago at this point. And I think I just gravitated towards that type of work and Tony recognized that superpower in me even though I don't have that formal training. So yeah, I'm a bit of an artist for fun, but I guess a data scientist in practice or for career. (00:30:31): But I think that that non-traditional background has been a great thing because I'm able to hire people who have the technical skills that I don't have, the folks with PhDs in statistics and the data scientists, machine learning and otherwise. I am able to hire those folks and yet keep them really focused on driving business impact because my background was on the finance side, and so I've always been a pragmatist. And for me, the purpose of our team is to drive business impact. And so the mix between the technical skills of the smarter people that I've hired, the smarter than myself, and my grounding in driving business impact has been a really great partnership.
turns.zh:
是啊，这挺有趣的。我常开玩笑说，我得到这份工作是因为传统数据科学背景不足，而非自身能力。不过我知道伊丽莎白·斯通在她与你的播客中多次谈到她作为首席技术官的非传统背景。所以，或许这其中确有其因。但我当初成为数据科学家纯属无奈之举。在DoorDash早期（约十年前），我完全自学了SQL和Python技术，因为公司急需有人帮助制定正确的目标、设定绩效指标，并分析不同市场的表现。托尼尽管看重我的实践能力，但我毕竟没有正规培训背景。不过说真的，我在业余时间倒是挺有艺术细胞的，但职业生涯里我始终是一名务实的数据科学家。

（00:30:31）不过这种非传统背景反倒成了优势——我能招到具备我所欠缺的技术专长的员工，比如统计学博士、数据科学家、机器学习专家等。我既能聘请这些人才，又能确保他们专注于业务价值的提升，因为我有金融领域的从业背景，所以向来务实。对我而言，团队的核心使命就是创造商业价值。将我招募的比我更优秀的技术人才与我深厚的业务洞察力相结合，形成了一种极其高效的协作模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's quite an inspiring story for someone that is just starting out and doesn't necessarily have a lot of experience in data, but also just generally. I think this is a really cool example. You could be successful in a field that you don't have a ton of background in. I'm curious what you think it was in you that allowed you to succeed in this and get to where you are today. What do you think you did right or what is some habits or ways of thinking that you think helped you achieve that?
turns.zh: 对于刚入行且缺乏数据领域深厚经验的人，甚至对所有人来说，这都是一个非常鼓舞人心的故事。我认为这是一个绝佳的范例。即便你不具备某个领域的深厚背景，也能在其中取得成功。我很好奇，是你身上的哪些特质助你达成今天的成就？你认为自己做对了哪些事情，或者有哪些思维习惯或方法对你的成功有所助益？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: First off, I have imposter syndrome like everybody else. So it's not like I have this crazy sense of confidence of like, "Oh, I can do anything." I definitely have the same doubts that others have. I think part of it was probably not even realizing what I was doing. When you're at a startup and things are moving quickly and you see a problem, and I've always liked solving problems, so I was like, "All right, how do I solve this problem?" It was like, "Oh, well, I need access to the data. I don't have access to the data. All right, I'll ask an engineer to get me the data. Well, this isn't going to scale. I can't always bother an engineer, so how do I figure out how to get the data myself? Well, let's learn Python." So I think it happened organically and I don't think I realized at the time what I was even doing. (00:32:41): And then I think if you think about things from first principles about what you need right now in front of you to unblock yourself or solve a problem, and you just focus on that instead of thinking about a global org that you're trying to build. I think that that helps. So for me, it was always about solving the problem in front of me the best way I could. And if that meant I needed to hire an engineer to report into me through the finance org, then that was what we were going to do and nobody was going to tell me I couldn't do it. So I think it's a belief in yourself, and ultimately it's just my desire to solve problems and figure out what has to get done is, I think, ultimately how it came about.
turns.zh: 首先，我和其他人一样都有冒名顶替综合症。所以我并没有那种自视甚高的感觉，觉得自己无所不能。我和其他人一样也会有同样的疑虑。我想部分原因可能在于我当时甚至没有意识到自己在做什么。当你在一家初创公司，事情进展迅速，你看到一个问题，而我一直喜欢解决问题，所以我就想：“好吧，我该怎么解决这个问题？”比如，“哦，嗯，我需要访问数据，但我没有权限。好吧，我会让工程师帮我获取数据。不过这玩意儿没法扩展，我又不能总是麻烦工程师，那我该怎么自己获取数据呢？嗯，那就学Python吧。”所以我觉得这都是自然而然发生的，我当时甚至没有意识到自己在做什么。（00:32:41）：然后我认为，如果你从第一性原理出发，思考当前眼前需要什么才能突破困境或解决问题，而不是去考虑你正试图建立的全球性组织。我觉得这很有帮助。所以对我来说，一直都是尽最大努力解决眼前的问题。如果这意味着我需要雇一个工程师，让他通过财务部门向我汇报，那我们就这么做，没有人能告诉我不行。所以我认为这是一种对自己的信念，最终还是源于我渴望解决问题，弄清楚必须做什么，我想这就是成功的秘诀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that so much. There's so many elements there that I think a lot of people can learn from. I feel like there's also this underlying current of you're just motivated for this to work. You wanted DoorDash to succeed, and you're just like, "I will do what I need to do to make this happen. I need to solve these problems. I'm not going to overthink. Do I have the skills necessarily to do these things [inaudible 00:33:48]?"
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这段话了。里面有很多元素，我觉得很多人都能从中学习。我感觉还有一种潜在的动力，就是你就是想让这件事成功。你希望DoorDash成功，然后你就想：“我要做我需要做的，才能让这件事成功。我需要解决这些问题。我不会想太多。[00:33:48不清]我有必要的技能来做这些事吗？”

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, I think I'm competitive. I think that's a trait that you find in a lot of early DoorDash folks and current DoorDash folks, to be honest, just wanting to win and being willing to do whatever you need to win. So roll up your sleeves, do something that's not your job. I think back to early days of taking out the garbage on Saturday nights because it needed to get done. I think that that was something that is ingrained in our culture from Tony Xu, from our founder and CEO, and I think that really resonated with me, and I feel like I've always operated that way as well. And I think that that helped me in my career to be able to do what I've done without really thinking about it too much.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得我很有竞争意识。我觉得这是很多早期DoorDash员工和现任DoorDash员工共有的特质，就是想赢，愿意为胜利付出一切。所以挽起袖子，做一些不属于你职责的事。我回想起早期周六晚上倒垃圾的日子，因为这些事必须完成。我觉得这就是从我们的创始人兼CEO徐 Tony Xu 那里传承下来的文化，深深根植于我们的基因里，我觉得这对我影响很大，我也一直这样做事。所以这也帮助我在职业生涯中能够做到现在这些事，而无需过多思考。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any other memories or stories of the early days of DoorDash that would be fun to share? Something that sticks with you of like, "Wow, I can't believe that's what it was like?"
turns.zh: 有没有其他关于DoorDash早期的回忆或故事，分享出来会很有趣？比如让你感叹“哇，真不敢相信当时是这样”的那种？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Oh man, there's so many, including so many mistakes that we've made. But I think something that really stands out to me is before I moved to the analytics area, I was actually a GM. I was the first GM at DoorDash and I was in Boston in 2014 launching the city of Boston when nobody knew who we were. And we would wake up early in the morning, 5 A.M. and we would go out, it was the winter of 2014. We'd go out and we'd hand out promo codes consumers outside of the [inaudible 00:35:30] in Boston, and these promo cards would be attached to kind bars so people would take them. And the whole team, it was a small team, there were four of us, but the whole team would go out in the morning to do this. And I think back to our sales guy, shout out to Joey G. So Joe Graccio is our sales guy in Boston-
turns.zh: 天哪，遇到的挑战太多了，包括我们犯过的诸多错误。但有一件事让我印象特别深刻。在转到分析部门之前，我曾担任过总经理。我是DoorDash首位总经理，2014年在波士顿启动业务时，我们还默默无闻。当时是冬天，早上5点我们就出门发送优惠码，这些优惠码附在巧克力棒上，方便路人领取。整个团队规模很小，只有四个人，但我们每天早上都会集体外出宣传。还要特别提到我们的销售人员乔伊·G（Joey G.）——他在波士顿市场开拓商家资源方面表现出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:35:47] Joey G.

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: And he was gold on signing merchants on the platform. (00:35:55): That was how he was gold. His compensation was tied to that. And yet in the morning when we would go out, he was with us handing out promo codes because he was part of the team because he wanted to win. We wanted to grow the business. And I think that that is just a great example of the culture that Tony and the early employees and Stanley and Andy, other co-founders really instilled in all of us early in those days. So I think that that ownership, that extreme ownership of the outcome is definitely one of the things. (00:36:32): I think the other is just being very customer first. And I say customer, I mean consumers, dashers and merchants as all being our customers. And the first time I ever went to the office headquarters in Palo Alto, which at the time was in an animal hospital. The first time I went there, there was a huge site outage and the whole company, it was like 20 people at the time, the whole company jumped online to do customer support, to answer the phones, to make sure that folks were getting refunds for orders that weren't going through, make sure the orders that were out there were getting delivered, just dropped everything and hopped on to do support. (00:37:15): And I was brand new, didn't really know how to use the tools, and so it was like, "How can I be useful?" And so back in those days, we used to order dinner to the office using DoorDash. And so in order to preserve about three dashers who would've had to deliver food to us, I was like, "I'm going to go out, go out dashing, go get everyone pizza so that we could feed the masses doing credits and refunds and do what we had to to make sure that we were serving our customers well." And I think that night was one of the largest refunds as a percent of our bank account that we had ever given out. And I think Tony, there were two examples that he's talked about where we just gave a lot of money back to customers because it was the right thing to do because our service failed and we wanted to do right by them. (00:38:06): So I think that those are two stories that stick out in my mind and really highlight culturally what makes DoorDash unique and what I think has been a really important part of our success.
turns.zh:
他在签约商家方面堪称高手（00:35:55）。他的薪酬与业绩挂钩。即便早晨外出宣传时，他也会和我们一起发送优惠码，因为他是团队的一员，志在共赢。我们想拓展业务。我认为这正是托尼、早期员工、斯坦利和安迪等联合创始人在早期为我们注入的文化精髓。这种对结果的极度负责，绝对是关键所在。（00:36:32）另一核心理念就是以客户为先。所谓客户，既包括消费者、外卖员，也包括商家。我第一次去帕洛阿尔托总部时，那时公司还设在一家宠物医院。第一次去那里，公司遭遇了大规模系统故障。当时只有20名员工，全员上线提供客户支持，接听电话，确保未成功的订单退款，保证已下单的订单按时配送，所有人放下手头工作，全力支援。

（00:37:15）我当时新人一个，完全不会用工具，心里想：“我能帮上什么忙？”于是我们开始用DoorDash为办公室订餐。为了节省三名外卖员为我们送餐的时间，我决定亲自外卖，帮大家买披萨，这样我们就能专心处理退款和退货事宜，确保为客户提供优质服务。我记得那晚我们发放的退款金额占银行账户比例创下新高。我想托尼提到的两个例子也很能说明问题——我们曾退还大量款项，因为服务出了问题，这是正确的选择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of the story that Tony and all the early employees, and I imagine you did this just like, "We're dashers," it's like a rotation where you dash for a while. Is that part of the culture?
turns.zh: 这让我想起托尼和早期员工的故事。我猜你们当时也这样做过：“我们也是外卖员啊。”这就像轮班制，先外卖一阵子。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, so we have a program, a WeDash program, and Keith Yandell, who's our chief business officer, did your podcast last year and he talked about this. But four times a year all the employees go out and go dashing or do customer support, and it's part of our culture that I love. I actually go pair dashing, so I go together with one of my colleagues. We've done it for years now, and it's a fun thing that we do together four times a year. Actually, usually more than that. And it's important because you get to use the product, you build empathy with all the audiences. I think all of us order DoorDash a lot, so we've built empathy with consumers. But being able to go and understand what it's like to go out dashing and when you're in the restaurant going and talking with merchants and seeing the experience from their point of view, I think it's just incredibly important. And of course we find a lot of bugs like, "Hmm, this doesn't work the way it should, let me report this." So I think it's also just great for catching bugs in the product.
turns.zh: 是的，我们有一个项目，叫WeDash项目。我们的首席商务官基思·扬德尔去年参加了你们的播客节目，他谈到了这个项目。但每年四次，全体员工都会出去送餐或提供客户支持服务。这是我们文化中我最喜欢的一部分。我实际上会和同事一起送餐合作。我们已经这样做了很多年了，这是一项我们每年四次共同参与的有趣活动。实际上，通常次数还不止于此。这很重要，因为你能亲自使用产品，增进对所有用户群体的理解。我想我们大家都经常使用DoorDash，所以我们与消费者之间建立了共鸣。但能够亲自去送餐，了解送餐者的感受，当你身处餐厅与商家交流时，从他们的视角看问题，我认为这非常重要。当然，我们还能发现很多漏洞，比如“嗯，这个功能不应该这样啊，让我去报告一下”。所以我认为这对发现产品漏洞也非常有帮助。
