It's like, "No. I mean, yes, you are a data scientist, but your goal is to figure out what's happening, and if that means that you're going to pick up the phone and call customers, then that is what you're going to do." And I think that expecting that and setting that as the norm for the team, this ownership of the outcome is something that we continue to do at DoorDash and instill in everyone whether you were early or just joined last month.
turns.zh: 我认为两者皆有。这绝对是文化层面的东西。我认为它源自高层领导，托尼就展现出这种极强的归属感，并在他人身上寻找这种特质。所以我认为这很有帮助。但即使在今天，我也期望我的团队对结果拥有同样的极强归属感。所以比起让某人被框定在某个角色里，我更感兴趣的是让团队想办法解决问题，而不是被框定在某个角色里。比如，“我是一名数据科学家，所以我只做这些事情。”对吧？而是，“不。我的意思是，是的，你是一名数据科学家，但你的目标是弄清楚正在发生什么，如果这意味着你要拿起电话给客户打电话，那你就应该去做。”我认为期望团队拥有这种归属感，并将其设定为团队的规范，这种对结果的归属感，是我们在DoorDash一直践行并灌输给每个人的东西，无论你是早期加入还是上个月才加入的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of that that comes to mind of someone practicing extreme ownership, like a data scientist calling someone or something along those lines?
turns.zh: 您能否举个例子，说明什么样的人在践行“极端所有权”理念？比如，数据科学家会给某人或某个部门打电话之类的？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, so I actually had a meeting yesterday morning with the team that's working on some of our affordability initiatives and we had shipped something that we expected to work, and it didn't. And instead of, "You can dig into the data," to understand the segments of consumers that you would expect it to work with and those that it wouldn't, of course we did that. But ultimately it was like, "I don't know why." And that's where qualitative research is superior to quantitative research, it's asking for the context, to actually talking to people to figure out what was the motivation, what worked, what didn't for them. And so the team, data scientists included, just sat and made phone calls. And so they were talking about what they found from those phone calls and that's going to inform future decisions. And I think rather than saying, "Well, that's what the qualitative research team is supposed to do," it's like, "No, no, no, that is what our team, anyone's team is supposed to do because that's what's needed to unblock us from this next test that we want to run because we need to know what we are testing." (00:43:23): So I think that it happens every day. I think I really love when I see team members go outside the traditional bounds of what a data science role might be and do some product management work, do some engineering work. I think that that's part of what keeps the job interesting. I think it's part of what makes our team special is that that is not only allowed, it's encouraged, and probably also a reason why we've had folks who've gone from my team to the product org and to the ops org and to the finance org is because they get to do and experience parts of that job and get a good sense for what that's like and then realize it's something that they love. So I think it's definitely something we encourage at DoorDash.
turns.zh: 是的，昨天上午我和负责可负担性计划的团队开了个会。我们推出了一个本以为能有效的方案，结果却不尽如人意。不是让他们去深入分析数据，找出预期有效的消费者群体和无效的群体——当然我们也这么做了。但最终还是会说：“我不知道为什么会这样。” 这时候定性研究就比定量研究更有优势了，它需要深入了解背景，真正与人交流，搞清楚他们的动机是什么，有什么地方做对了，有什么地方做错了。所以团队成员，包括数据科学家们，就坐下来打电话。然后他们会聊聊从这些电话中发现的问题，这些信息将为未来的决策提供参考。我觉得不能简单地说“这就是定性研究团队该做的事”，而是应该说：“不，不，不，这是我们团队、任何团队都该做的事，因为这正是我们解开下一步测试困局所需要的。” （00:43:23）所以我觉得这种情况每天都在发生。我特别喜欢看到团队成员突破数据科学角色的传统界限，参与产品管理工作，甚至工程开发工作。我认为这正是这份工作保持趣味性的原因之一，也是我们团队的独特之处——不仅允许这样做，还积极鼓励这样做。这或许也是为什么有员工从我的团队转到产品部门、运营部门、财务部门的原因，因为他们能接触到这些工作的不同方面，对其本质有深刻理解，最终意识到自己热爱这份工作。所以在DoorDash，我们绝对鼓励这种跨界尝试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I want to move in a slightly different direction. One of your colleagues told me that you are incredibly good at defining metrics, which is so important to get right for a business, especially when it's complex at DoorDash. And I hear you're especially good at finding the right metric to drive the right incentive, especially when the business is really messy and things like that. So I'm just curious what you've learned about how to pick good metrics and align incentives well.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这一点。接下来我想问个不同方向的问题。您的一位同事告诉我，您非常擅长定义指标，这对企业的运营至关重要，尤其是在DoorDash这样复杂的环境中。我听说您特别善于找到正确的指标来驱动合适的激励措施，尤其是在业务非常混乱的情况下。所以我很好奇，您在选择有效指标和合理设计激励机制方面有什么心得？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: I've learned a lot of things about metrics, mostly from bad metrics. I actually think you learn a lot from picking the wrong metric. Ultimately, you want to find a short-term metric you can measure that drives a long-term output. So people always talk about, "Oh, we want to drive an improvement in retention." Retention is a terrible thing to goal on because it's almost impossible to drive in a meaningful way in the short term, and yet you want to be able to experiment and iterate quickly. So what are the things that drive retention? What are the inputs? So I think it's really important to find the right inputs, and then through experimentation test whether or not those short-term inputs are driving the long-term output that you're looking for. I think that's one thing. I think keeping things simple is another thing I've learned over the years, maybe it's data scientists, but they tend to love these composite metrics with a coefficient. (00:45:44): "We're going to wait this input at X and this input at X+2." And then you end up with a metric that nobody really understands that doesn't actually mean anything. And you're like, "I don't know if a 0.1 increase is it a lot? Is it good? Is it bad?" So they're just hard to work with. (00:46:07): And so I always encourage folks, just pick something simple, even if it's not perfect and your composite would be more perfect. If people understand it, if they have an intuition around it, if it's something that people can talk about across the company, it's going to be a much better metric in terms of driving real outcomes than your made up composite score that nobody understands. So I think keeping things simple is also really important. And then I think the last thing I'll say is it's important to understand how metrics across the company equate to one another. (00:46:43): And so we spend a lot of time quantifying things in terms of a common currency. So for example, if I were to lower price by a dollar, what would I get in terms of, we'll say, volume? Well, what if I lowered delivery times by a minute? What do I get for that in terms of volume? And so now you can make trade-offs between maybe your marketing team and your logistics team because you have this common currency that everyone can talk about. And so we've done that. We've tried to quantify all of the levers of our business, price, selection, quality in common terms, so that if we have, say, a dollar to spend, we know what we get depending on where we put it, over what timeframe. I think that that helps us make decisions more quickly because we know what our options are. We know we have our inventory of things that we can do, short-term, long-term, and what we get for it. So it definitely helps us to make decisions more quickly and hopefully better decisions.
turns.zh: 我学到了很多关于指标的知识，大多是从糟糕的指标中吸取的教训。实际上，我认为从选择错误的指标中也能收获很多。最终，你希望找到一个短期可衡量的指标，能推动长期的产出。所以人们总是说：“哦，我们想提高用户留存率。”但留存率是一个极难设定目标的指标，因为短期内很难以有意义的方式提升它。然而你又希望能快速进行实验和迭代。那么，哪些因素能驱动用户留存呢？输入条件是什么？我认为找到正确的输入条件至关重要，然后通过实验测试这些短期输入是否能推动你所期望的长期产出。这很重要。多年来，我还意识到另一件事——也许数据科学家们也深有体会，他们往往喜欢那些带有系数的复合指标。（00:45:44）：“我们要等待X时刻的这个输入和X+2时刻的这个输入。” 最终你得到一个没人真正理解、毫无意义的指标。你会想：“0.1%的增长算多？好还是坏？”所以这些指标很难操作。（00:46:07）：所以我总是鼓励大家选择简单的东西，即便它不完美，你的复合指标或许更完美。但只要人们能理解它，有直观认识，能在全公司范围内进行讨论，它就会比那些没人懂的复合评分更能推动实际成果。因此，保持简单性也非常重要。最后我想说的是，理解公司内各指标之间的关联也很重要。（00:46:43）：所以我们花大量时间将各种事物量化为通用货币。例如，如果我把价格降低一美元，销量会增加多少？如果我把交付时间缩短一分钟呢？这样一来，营销团队和物流团队就能进行权衡，因为大家都有一个可以交流的通用货币。我们已经这样做了。我们努力将业务的所有杠杆（价格、选品、质量）量化为通用术语，这样当我们有1美元预算时，就能根据不同投入在不同时间框架内的效果做出选择。我认为这有助于我们更快地做出决策，因为我们清楚自己的选择范围，知道可以利用的短期、长期资源，以及它们带来的回报。因此，这确实能帮助我们更快地做出决策，希望还能做出更明智的决策。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These are so awesome. I definitely want to follow up on some of this. This is so good. So maybe on this last one, which we did at Airbnb also like, how does everything translate into Knight's book and booking? Every decision we make, what is the actual Knight's book impact? And so I imagine in your case, I don't know if you want to talk about these things. I imagine it's transactions, or purchases, or GMB or something like that, so I'm guessing is the final metric. I don't know. Is that something you talk about or you don't talk about that?
turns.zh: 这些太棒了。我肯定想深入探讨其中一些内容。这太棒了。那么最后一个例子，我们在Airbnb也做过类似的尝试，比如，如何将所有指标与Knight的书和预订量关联起来？我们做的每个决策，实际对Knight的书有何影响？所以我猜在你们公司，我不知道你们是否愿意谈论这些内容。我猜是交易量、购买量、GMB之类的，最终指标应该是预订量吧？我不知道，你们是否谈论过这些？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: We measure things in terms of GOV, so Gross Order Value, and also volume.
turns.zh: 我们用GOV来衡量，即总订单价值，还有交易量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. [inaudible 00:48:34]. Okay, so basically every other metric that people are gold on as much as you can translate, there's a model that translates that into Gross Order Value and volume? Awesome. So when a team is saying, "Hey, we're going to change the onboarding flow and impact conversion here." I don't know. I guess what are some examples of other metrics on teams that potentially translate into GOV and volume just to make it even more real?
turns.zh: 明白了。[00:48:34的不可听清内容]。好的，基本上来说，人们关注的其他所有指标，只要能转化成毛订单价值和交易量的，都有对应的模型吧？太棒了。所以当一个团队说"嘿，我们要改进新用户引导流程，提升转化率"之类的，我不知道，你能不能举些例子，说明其他团队的哪些指标可能转化为毛订单价值和交易量，这样更直观些？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah. So everything from the example that you started with, which is an improvement in the login flow, how many more consumers are getting onto the app and ultimately placing orders. And so you can translate that to, of course, orders and GOV. But then something as interesting as selling a Thai restaurant in Sacramento, we're able to say, "What do we think that that gets us in terms of GOV from the consumer by selling that Thai restaurant?" So it's every area of the business, it's mobilizing more dashers on the road. What does that do to our quality metrics in terms of delivery times? How does that translate? So because of that, we're able to figure out if we want to spend the dollar or spend the time, the team's time, on improving conversion or spending more money in marketing or onboarding more dashers or signing more restaurants or adding more grocery stores. So we are able to look across the whole business and figure out what is the right mix of actions to take to achieve our goals.
turns.zh: 是的。从你提到的例子开始，比如改进登录流程，让更多用户下载应用并下单。然后这些数据就能转化为订单量和毛订单价值了。还有一些更有趣的案例，比如在萨克拉门托卖泰国餐厅，我们可以分析通过卖这家泰国餐厅，能为公司带来多少毛订单价值？这适用于业务的方方面面，比如调动更多外卖骑手上路，这会对我们的配送时效等质量指标产生什么影响？如何量化这些影响？基于此，我们就能判断是该投入资金还是人力，提升转化率，还是加大营销投入，或者增加骑手数量、签约更多餐厅、开设更多生鲜超市。这样我们就能统筹全局，找到实现目标的最优策略组合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could see as you talk about this why this is so important in a marketplace, especially a multi-sided marketplace where there's always trade-off decisions between supply investment and demand growth and dasher growth. I don't even know, my brain would explode trying to think about all these things, so I get exactly why this is so important to business. Okay. And then in terms of the simple recommendation, I think when people hear like, "Yeah, keep it simple," they're like, "Yeah, yeah, we're going to keep it simple." What are some things that point to, "This is not simple," that tell you like, "No, this is way too complicated. You should try to simplify this metric even though it's not ideal. It's not the perfect metric, but it needs to be simpler."
turns.zh: 听你讲这些，我能理解为什么这在市场平台上如此重要，尤其是在多边市场中，供给投资、需求增长和骑手增长之间总是存在权衡取舍。我甚至觉得，要是把所有这些因素都考虑清楚，我的脑子肯定会炸掉。所以我完全明白这对业务有多重要。好的。那关于简化指标的建议，我觉得人们听到“保持简单”时，通常会说“是啊，是啊，我们要保持简单”。但有些情况会让人意识到“这并不简单”，比如“不行，这太复杂了。你应该简化这个指标，虽然它不完美，但必须更简单易懂。”

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah. So we had a score for merchant health, which we tried experimenting with, which was a combination of factors that we had found would lead to a merchant being on the platform and getting an order. So we wanted to make sure that the merchant had active hours on the platform and had images and had a full menu that was accurate and robust. A number of different inputs. And we created a composite that weighted all of these different inputs. And then we were like, "What is our merchant health score?" And you were like, "It's 0.35. It's not 35%. So what is that, that 0.35? I don't know what it is." So instead of that, we said, "What are the most important factors in order... First, let's measure how many of the new merchants are getting an order within their first, say, seven days on the platform. (00:51:57): And then let's look at how many of our merchants are doing these things we know are important. So these inputs. So let's goal our team on getting merchant photo coverage up. Let's goal the team on making sure that we have open hours, accurate hours." So yes, someone might say it's simpler to have a composite metric, but it was so hard to understand what it was and how to move it that it became meaningless. And ultimately moving to something that was simpler to understand, even if it meant having three metrics instead of one, it ultimately was better for the team because folks knew what they were trying to move. And so yeah, maybe we missed number four, five and six on the list of things, but you got one through three and that's 95% of it anyway. So once we get success with that 95, then let's talk about figuring out the other 5%.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我们曾推出一个商家健康评分机制，尝试用它来衡量商家在平台上的活跃度以及获取订单的概率。具体来说，我们综合了多个因素，比如商家在平台上的活跃时段、图片展示、菜单信息的准确性和完整性等。我们创建了一个综合评分模型，对这些不同因素进行加权评估。然而，用户对这个评分机制的理解存在困难，比如“商家健康评分到底是多少？”用户可能误解为“0.35”是百分比，但实际上这是0.35分。我们不得不重新调整思路：首先，重点监测新入驻商家在平台首七天内获得订单的比例；其次，确保所有商家都做好了关键优化，比如完善图片展示、调整营业时间等。最终，我们将团队目标聚焦于提升商家图片覆盖率和营业时间准确性等核心指标。虽然这意味着需要同时管理三个指标而非一个综合评分，但团队更容易理解并推进优化工作。毕竟，95%的关键指标已达成，剩余5%的优化空间可逐步推进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so funny because this is exactly what we went through at Airbnb, we had, we call that a healthy host. I led the host quality team for a while and we came up with this healthy host metric that was six factors of a host, like the cancellation rate, the review rate, their response rate and things like that. And then we're just like, "Cool, let's move this, let make more hosts healthy." And then you end up like, "Okay, which one do we focus on?," And, "Oh, what about all these others?" And we ended up basically focusing on one at a time. And so let's just make that the goal for now and then rotate through the different biggest [inaudible 00:53:28] opportunities to move. [inaudible 00:53:30].
turns.zh: 这真有趣，我们在Airbnb也遇到过类似问题。我们曾推出“健康房东”评分标准，将房东的取消率、评价率、回复率等六项指标纳入考量。结果却陷入纠结：“重点关注哪项指标？”“其他指标怎么办？” 最终我们选择逐一突破。例如，先专注于某个关键指标，待优化完成再转向下一个。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Exactly. I think in hindsight for the example you give, which of those six things are actually the most important? And if you're able to then quantify which one matters most, you work on that one first and you materially move that one and then you work on the next one. You want to move them all. But being able to prioritize and know what you're going to get for a 20% improvement in, say, your cancellation rate, that's where analytics I think can add a lot of value. Because yes, ultimately you'll get to all of them, but the way you do that and the time can have a meaningful impact on your growth. If you can target the most problematic things first and solve those, you get more bang for your buck and that compounds over time. And so doing the things that matter first and most quickly is a competitive advantage in my opinion.
turns.zh: 确实如此。回顾案例，六项指标中哪些最重要？若能量化最关键的因素，先攻克核心问题，再逐项推进。用户希望同时优化所有指标，但优先级管理至关重要。例如，提升20%的取消率所需的分析价值远超其他指标。先解决最紧迫的问题，事半功倍，长期来看能形成良性循环。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thing we found along those same lines is rotating between different metrics is so not efficient because you get good at, "We're going to move this metric." And your team's like, "Cool, we totally understand this lever," like cancellation rate. We become really smart at cancellation rate and then three months later, you need to switch to response rate and they have to learn a whole new paradigm of how to think about it. And it's just super inefficient. So we found basically, just keep a team on the metric until there's no more opportunities and give another team one of these other metrics.
turns.zh: 我们还发现，在同一个领域内频繁切换不同的衡量标准效率极低。比如，你刚掌握了一个衡量标准，团队就开始兴致勃勃地说：“我们要调整这个指标！”但三个月后，你又得改成另一个指标，他们又得重新学习全新的思维模式。这实在太低效了。所以我们的做法是，直到某个团队对某个指标已经无计可施时，再交给另一个团队处理。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So many lessons. Okay. And the first thing you said on how to pick a good metric about this idea of short-term metrics that have long-term impact. How did you phrase that again?
turns.zh: 学到太多了。好的。你之前提到的如何选择一个好的衡量标准，特别是那些具有长期影响的短期指标。你具体怎么说的来着？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, so we find proxy metrics for long-term outcomes.
turns.zh: 对，我们会为长期结果找寻替代衡量标准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And it's similar to the simple metric, and it all comes down to, again, just like the metric should be something probably, you can move, you can understand, that's close enough to this ideal, perfect metric, but isn't necessarily the entire ideal. Okay, awesome. Anything else along these lines of just picking metrics, working with metrics that you've learned that would be worth [inaudible 00:55:28]?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这和简单衡量标准的理念很相似，关键在于，衡量标准应该易于理解、易于操作，尽可能接近理想的完美衡量标准，但不必追求完美。好的，很棒。还有其他关于选择衡量标准、处理已学到的衡量标准的经验值得分享吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: With metrics, we are often looking at the average, and I think we talked about this a little bit earlier, but making sure that you're looking at the edge cases and your fail states is also really important. And so we often will set goals actually and create metrics around those edge cases. So like the disaster deliveries, the ones that go terribly wrong. So we have this concept of Never Delivered, which is orders that are never delivered. We're really great at naming things at DoorDash, and they're very rare. And so if you were just looking at the average effect or the average consumer experience, it would never come up. If you were just measuring quality based on average values of delivery times and lateness [inaudible 00:56:18], these wouldn't show up because they are so rare, but they're terrible. They're terrible experiences for consumers. They lead to churn. (00:56:27): They're incredibly expensive because you're refunding an order or repurchasing food and having to send another dasher to deliver that repurchased food. So they're very expensive, they're costly from a consumer experience standpoint. And I think if you're not looking for these fail states, they are often missed. So I think when you're picking metrics, yes, you want to improve engagement and you want to improve conversion, and there's a lot of things that are averages overall that you want to move, but it's so important to find these edge cases in these fail states and actually set concrete goals around eliminating them because it can be really powerful.
turns.zh: 在衡量标准方面，我们经常关注平均值。我想我们之前稍微提到过，但确保关注边缘案例和失败状态也非常重要。因此，我们经常设定目标，并围绕这些边缘案例创建衡量标准。比如灾难性配送任务——那些严重出错的订单。在DoorDash，我们对这些情况有专门的命名，比如“从不配送”（指永远未能配送成功的订单）。我们很擅长给这些情况起名字，但它们确实非常罕见。如果你只看平均效果或平均消费者体验，可能根本注意不到这些问题。比如，如果你仅根据平均配送时间和延迟来衡量质量，这些问题就不会显现出来，因为它们太罕见了。但它们确实很糟糕，对消费者来说是极坏的体验，会导致客户流失。（00:56:27）它们成本极高，因为你得退款、重新购买食物，还得派新的外卖员去重新配送。总之，从消费者体验角度看，它们代价巨大。如果你不关注这些失败状态，很容易忽视它们。所以在选择衡量标准时，除了提升用户参与度和转化率，还有很多平均值指标需要改进，但找到这些边缘案例和失败状态，并设定明确的消除目标，效果会显著得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the tip here is actually make that a goal like, never deliver at some team, just keep cutting that down?
turns.zh: 所以这里的建议就是，把这作为一个目标，比如某个团队永远不配送失败的订单，然后不断优化？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Exactly. So we have part of our quality analytics team and we have product engineering and ops on it as well. Their goal is to eradicate Never Delivered. And in order to do that, you have to understand why they happen. Sometimes it's human error, sometimes it's fraud. And then figure out ways that you can prevent them, that you can fix them while it's happening and ultimately just get rid of them from the system. And you're never going to completely get rid of them, but you can make a meaningful impact to make them even more rare than a fraction of a percent.
turns.zh: 没错。所以我们有部分质量分析团队成员，还有产品工程和运营人员参与其中。他们的目标是彻底消除“未送达”问题。而要做到这一点，就必须先理解这种情况发生的原因。有时是人为失误，有时是欺诈行为。然后要想办法预防这些问题，及时纠正现有问题，最终将其从系统中彻底清除。虽然永远无法彻底消除这些问题，但我们可以通过有效措施将其发生率降至远低于千分之一的水平。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And I feel like people may be hearing this and like, "Of course, why would you not focus on terrible work experiences?" But I think in most companies, they look at the big numbers, they look at the averages as you said like, "Oh, it almost never happens. Why do we even spend any time on this?" And your point is, you should actually spend time on these really terrible experiences, even if it's a tiny portion of your business. I guess maybe share why that's important. Is it just because that has trickle-down effects on the brand?
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得人们听到这些可能会想：“当然，难道不应该专注于糟糕的客户体验吗？”但我认为在大多数公司里，他们只看大数据，只看平均值。比如他们会说：“哦，这种情况几乎不会发生，我们为什么还要在这上面浪费时间？”而你的观点是，实际上应该花时间关注这些极其糟糕的体验，即便它们只占业务的一小部分。我猜你能否解释一下为什么这很重要？是因为这会对品牌形象产生连锁反应吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, I think it's a couple of things. So just because something doesn't happen frequently doesn't mean that it's not important. So the Never Delivered example is a great one in that this is leading directly to churn and it's also costing a lot of money far more than its frequency would suggest. And I think the fact of the matter is is when you have things that cause churn, you're losing all of that consumer's subsequent orders, and that is not necessarily observed. You're just seeing one bad experience, you're not seeing all of the lost orders because they're lost. And so I think that sometimes this is an area where the data doesn't show you the full picture. And being able to quantify the impact on engagement, on profitability, will make it stand out as something that really, that you would maybe miss if you weren't really looking for it. (00:59:25): And then I think the other thing is with something like login errors, sometimes you don't see it in the data because people can't even get into the data. If you're not able to log in, you're not making any purchases, you're not ordering, and so you may not see it in the data that you're looking at. And so that's also something that I think is important for data folks to think about, which is what data don't we have? What data might we be missing? Where might there be opportunities and things that we actually need to identify and fix that we may not see? Because in this case, with login failures, they're not able to log in. They're not in the denominator, and so we're missing out on them from the data set entirely.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得有几个方面的原因。某件事发生得不频繁并不意味着它不重要。“未送达”案例就是一个很好的例子，因为这直接导致客户流失，而且其造成的损失远超其发生频率所应承担的责任。关键在于，当出现导致客户流失的问题时，会失去所有后续订单，而这往往被忽视了。你只看到一次糟糕的体验，却看不到所有流失的订单，因为它们已经流失了。所以我认为有时候数据并不能完整呈现全貌。能够量化对用户参与度和盈利能力的影响，才会让这些问题凸显出来，否则你可能根本不会注意到它们。（00:59:25）：然后我觉得还有一点，关于登录错误的问题，有时数据里看不到这些问题，因为用户根本无法登录。如果登录不了，就无法进行购买或下单，所以你看到的数据里可能没有这些记录。因此，我认为数据团队需要思考的问题是，哪些数据我们没有？哪些数据可能被遗漏了？哪里有机会和问题需要我们识别并解决？因为在登录失败的情况下，用户无法登录，他们不在分母里，因此我们完全无法从数据集中获取这些信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just a couple of more questions. There's one that I skipped that I'm just going to come back to. It's completely out of nowhere, but I think it might be interesting is about a global data org. So you run a global data org, you have data scientists and analysts and biz ops people all over the world, not just the US. I'm curious just how is it different managing data people in different countries versus just the US? What's a big difference?
turns.zh: 再问几个问题。有一个我跳过了，现在再回来。这个问题完全出乎意料，但我觉得可能很有意思，关于全球数据组织的。你们运营着全球数据组织，在世界各地（不只是美国）都有数据科学家、分析师和商业运营人员。我很好奇，在不同国家管理数据团队和在美国管理相比，有什么不同之处？最大的区别是什么？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Everyone always asks about the differences. What I am surprised by is how similar things are, how similar people are, the data scientists themselves, but also consumers and dashers and couriers, as we call them at Volt. There's a lot more similarities than differences. I do think that when you built a business in the US and then you introduce new countries, having different currencies and different languages adds complexity that you weren't necessarily familiar with. I think similarly in EU countries versus non-EU countries in Europe, there's different regulation. So that adds a fun layer of complexity. So I do think that it adds complexity to the problem set, but ultimately so many of the problems are the same. It feels a little bit like going into a test having seen the answer key. And so for me, there are problems we've encountered at Volt through Volt analytics where I'm like, "Oh, we've had a similar problem. (01:01:49): I have an instinct for what the answer might be. Let's still test because there could be differences cultural or otherwise, but I feel like I know where we're going to end." And then sometimes there are problems where it's new for one reason or another, and it's exciting because you're like, "All right, let's see if things are different here." Let's see what ideas might work in a Volt country that don't work in a DoorDash country and vice versa. So I think I tend to focus more on what's the same, and then I'm pleasantly surprised when I find things that are different because that keeps you on your toes and keeps things interesting.
turns.zh: 大家总是问起各国之间的差异。但让我惊讶的是，无论是业务模式、数据科学家群体，还是消费者、外卖骑手和快递员（在Volt我们称他们为"Dashers"），各国之间其实有很多相似之处。相似之处远多于差异。我认为，当你在美国建立业务后，再向其他国家拓展时，汇率和语言差异确实会增加原本不熟悉的复杂性。同样，欧盟国家与非欧盟国家在监管方面也存在差异，这又增添了一层有趣的复杂性。所以我确实认为这会让问题变得更复杂，但归根结底，许多核心挑战都是相似的。这就像在考试中提前看到答案，心里已经有底。虽然有时候也会遇到新问题，但只要能找到相似之处，比如"我们之前也遇到过类似问题，可能答案相似"，或者"虽然这里有文化差异，但核心思路应该是一样的"，都会让我倍感欣慰。反之，遇到全新的挑战时，比如"这里和DoorDash的玩法不同"，也会激发我的探索欲望，探索在Volt的市场中行之有效的方案在DoorDash却行不通的例子。所以我更倾向于关注共性，当发现差异时也会倍感惊喜，因为这能时刻保持专注，让工作充满趣味。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to take us to AI Corner. This is a segment we have in the podcast where I try to understand how people are using AI in their day-to-day and in their business. I'm curious if you've found some really interesting way of using AI ideally in... you can go in either one of these directions, and how you or your team work day-to-day using AI tools to make you more efficient, or integrating AI into your product, making DoorDash better.
turns.zh: 接下来我们进入AI角。这是播客中的一个环节，我想了解大家如何在日常工作和业务中应用AI。我很想听听，你们是否找到了一些非常有趣的AI应用方式，或者团队如何通过AI工具提高效率，或者如何将AI融入产品，让DoorDash变得更出色。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, I think that there are opportunities in both. I think one of the things I'm really excited about is actually the former. So in helping to make the team more productive, we do something called Office Hours at DoorDash, the analytics team. And it's something that we started eight years ago, and it was a way to provide support for teams that at the time we just didn't have the bandwidth to support. So we would go, in the early days, we'd go sit in a room and we'd say, "Come on in and we'll help you with anything you need help with. We'll help teach you SQL. We'll help look at some of your work. We'll be a thought partner. You could just come learn what we're working on." Whatever it was. We would do two hours every week of Office Hours at different times to be friendly to different time zones. (01:03:52): And I think one of the things I'm excited about is being able to really empower some of the folks that are still coming to Office Hours for one thing or another to be able to use AI to help edit queries on their own for example, to be able to say, "Here's a query. I want to make this. Please adjust this to our grocery business so that I can see the GOV for grocery." And so working to build these tools that will help not just our team in terms of time saving, and also to be honest, folks are going to use it on our team, but really to be able to empower non-technical users to be able to do things on their own and not have to take up bandwidth for the analytics team.
turns.zh:
是的，我认为两者都有机会。让我特别兴奋的是前者。在帮助团队提高生产力方面，我们在DoorDash分析团队推行了一个叫做“办公时间”的项目。这个项目始于八年前，旨在为当时我们没有精力支持的团队提供支持。早期时，我们会坐在一个房间里，告诉大家：“随时来找我们吧，无论你需要什么帮助，我们都会教你SQL，帮你审阅工作成果，还能成为你的智囊。只要来学习我们的项目进展就行。”无论是哪种需求，我们每周都会在不同时段举办两小时的“办公时间”活动，以适应不同时区的需求。

（01:03:52）我最期待的是能真正赋能那些因各种原因仍来参加“办公时间”的同事。比如，他们可以用AI自主编辑查询语句，例如：“这里有个查询，我想针对我们的生鲜业务进行调整，让我能看到生鲜业务的GMV数据。” 我们致力于开发这些工具，不仅能为团队节省时间（说实话，我们团队也会用到），更能让非技术用户自主完成任务，无需占用分析团队的精力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So essentially it's a chatbot that anyone in the company can talk to you to get advice on how to write SQL queries, query data and things like that?
turns.zh: 所以本质上，这是一个公司内部的聊天机器人，任何人都可以找它获取如何编写SQL查询、查询数据等方面的建议？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a clever name for this chatbot per chance?
turns.zh: 这个聊天机器人有没有一个巧妙的名字？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: So it's not clever. It's called Ask Data AI, and that's named for our internal Slack channel that used to be the open Q&A for people to ask data. So it's not at all clever.
turns.zh: 其实并不巧妙。它叫Ask Data AI，这个名字来源于我们内部的Slack频道，这个频道曾用于开放式问答，方便大家提问数据相关的问题。所以名字一点也不巧妙。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But it's clear.
turns.zh: 但很清晰。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: But again, it goes with the theme of very, very specific naming conventions that we have at DoorDash; Never Delivered and Ask Data AI.
turns.zh: 不过说回来，它和DoorDash非常特定的命名约定很契合；比如Never Delivered和Ask Data AI。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Just clarity above all else. That's something I've learned from an editor that I work with. Jess, is there anything else that you want to share or leave listeners with? For folks that are trying to build their data teams, make their data teams more efficient, is there any final wisdom nugget you'd want to share?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个名字。首要的是清晰明了。这是我从合作的编辑那里学到的。杰斯，你还有什么想和听众分享的吗？对于那些正努力打造数据团队、提高数据团队效率的人，你有什么最终的智慧之言想分享吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: I think the only thing that I want to reiterate is that you don't necessarily need a formal training in whatever it is you're building. And I think that also goes towards the folks that you hire onto the team. And so I mentioned earlier that we've had a lot of folks go to product or go to ops from the team. What I didn't mention is how many folks we've actually had join the analytics team from partner teams. So whether that was from engineering or from our ops team or marketing or finance, we are a net importer of talent as opposed to a net exporter of talent. And I think that that's because my own experience coming over from operations, from being a GM and making that transition into analytics, I find that I'm drawn to other folks who want to make a similar transition. (01:06:39): Now again, you have to have the technical skills, and most of these folks have acquired these skills on the job, whatever job they are doing at DoorDash before they transition to the analytics team, or they had maybe some formal training in school. But I love seeing the folks that make that transition and actually want to join the analytics team, even if they're not a career or data scientist. I think it creates a really unique environment where you have folks on the team from different backgrounds with different expertise who can teach each other things. So I can teach you how to build a discounted cash flow model in Excel, and I can learn how to make kick-ass slides from someone who has a background in consulting. And I can learn about common gotchas in statistics from someone who comes to us with a Master's or a PhD in statistics, and we've got our econometrics folks and we've got our economists. We just have a group of people with different backgrounds who can all teach each other how to be better. And we're not all carbon copies of each other.
turns.zh: 我想我唯一想重申的一点是，无论你正在开发的产品或项目，都不一定需要接受过正式的培训。这同样适用于你招入团队的成员。我之前提到过，我们团队中有很多人从其他岗位转向产品或运营岗位。但我没提到的是，从合作团队加入分析团队的人数更多。无论是来自工程部门、运营团队、市场营销还是财务部门，我们实际上是人才的净引入者，而非净输出者。我认为这源于我自己的经历——从运营岗位转向分析岗位时，我发现自己被那些渴望实现类似转型的同事所吸引。（01:06:39）现在，再次强调，你必须具备技术技能。这些人中的大多数都是在职场中习得这些技能的，无论他们在加入分析团队前在DoorDash担任何种职位，或许还接受过正规教育。但我乐于看到那些愿意转向分析团队的同事，即便他们并非职业数据科学家。我认为这营造了一个独特的环境——团队成员来自不同背景，拥有不同专长，他们可以互相学习。我可以教你如何在Excel中构建贴现现金流模型，也可以向擅长咨询的人学习如何制作出色的幻灯片，还能向拥有统计学硕士或博士学位的人学习统计学中的常见陷阱。我们有计量经济学专家和经济学家。团队成员背景各异，但都能互相提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm hearing is you try to optimize almost for a lot of different complementary skills and very different backgrounds almost.
turns.zh: 我听到的是，你们试图优化几乎各种互补技能和截然不同背景的人才。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Exactly. And also people who have experience at different size companies. I think I love folks from startups who have that hustle and grit, but I also love folks who've seen what scale looks like and can help us see around corners as far as what problems we will encounter as the business is growing. And I think it is not just about a diversity of skill and a diversity of background, it's also diversity of prior company and stage. That can be really a unique way to think about structuring your team so that you get the best of both worlds.
turns.zh: 没错。还有在不同规模公司有经验的人。我喜欢那些来自初创公司、充满干劲和韧性的人，但我也喜欢那些见识过规模是什么样子、能帮助我们预见业务增长过程中会遇到哪些问题的同事。我认为这不仅关乎技能的多样性和背景的多样性，还关乎之前公司规模和发展阶段的多样性。这或许是构建团队的独特思路，让你能两全其美。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Well, just when you thought we were done, we reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。嗯，就在你以为我们结束时，我们迎来了一个令人兴奋的闪电问答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: I am. Let's do it.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. Okay. First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 开始吧。好的。第一个问题，您向他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: I tend to read fiction, particularly historical fiction, and I love spy novels. So I think my brain is always in problem-solving mode even when reading. A recent book that I read that I enjoyed was The Rose Code by Kate Quinn, and it's about women code breakers in World War II, and I really enjoyed that. But rather than recommending a book... I guess I did just recommend a book, but rather than recommending another book, I am going to recommend the Libby app and supporting your local public library because I love the library and I love Libby, so I'll give that as my other recommendation.
turns.zh: 我通常喜欢读小说，尤其是历史小说和间谍小说。所以即使在阅读时，我的大脑也总处于解决问题的模式中。最近我读了一本很喜欢的书，叫《玫瑰密码》（The Rose Code），作者是凯特·奎因（Kate Quinn），讲述了二战期间女性密码破译者的故事，我非常喜欢这本书。不过我不想推荐一本书……好吧，我刚刚确实推荐了一本书，但我不打算再推荐另一本书了。我要推荐的是Libby应用程序和支持当地公共图书馆，因为我热爱图书馆，也喜欢Libby，所以这就是我的另一个推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautiful. Very on brand with sharing economy, company stuff. Libby. Cool. Okay, next question. Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 太棒了。非常符合共享经济和公司宣传的风格。Libby。酷。好的，下一个问题。最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, another one. I don't actually watch a lot of TV, definitely don't watch a lot of movies. In fact, haven't seen some of the movie greats. I get yelled at a lot by my friend. "I can't believe you haven't seen that." I tend to re-watch things, so series from the past, over and over again. I think it's just like how I shut my brain off. So I've recently re-watched The West Wing, which is one of my favorite shows of all time, probably for the 50th time.
turns.zh: 又来一个。我其实不怎么看电视，也不怎么看电影。事实上，我有些电影巨作都没看过。朋友经常对我发脾气：“真不敢相信你居然没看过那个。”我习惯反复看以前的剧集，这样能让大脑放松。比如最近我又重温了《白宫风云》（The West Wing），这是我最喜欢的剧集之一，可能已经是第50遍了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God.
turns.zh: 天哪。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: And Alias, which was a Jennifer Garner series from the early 2000s. Also, Spy. So I'm noticing a theme. I think I really love the spy genre. But yeah, I've watched those. They're both great, but not at all current.
turns.zh: 还有《双面女间谍》（Alias），这是2000年代初詹妮弗·加纳（Jennifer Garner）主演的剧集。还有《间谍风云》（Spy）。看来我有偏好间谍题材的趋势。不过是的，我都看过了。它们都很棒，但都不是当下热门的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect. Perfectly acceptable. Do you have a favorite product that you recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 完美。完全可以接受。你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: This is a bit of a curveball. So Korean sunscreens. So I burn really easily, so I have to wear sunscreen and I love Korean sunscreens. I was introduced to them by a friend of mine, and they're just far superior to what we have in the US. So I highly recommend people give Korean sunscreens a try, particularly there's a Beauty of Joseon on branded sunscreen. It's just amazing and is delightful to wear, which is important when you have to wear it every day.
turns.zh: 这问题有点出乎意料。说说韩国防晒霜吧。我很容易晒伤，所以必须涂防晒霜，而韩国防晒霜比美国的要好得多。我是被朋友安利的，真的强烈推荐大家试试，尤其是Joseon Beauty品牌的防晒霜。效果超棒，用起来很愉快，这很重要，毕竟每天都要涂。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've been trying to wear more sunscreen as I age, and so this is a really good tip. Was that a brand you recommended?
turns.zh: 随着年龄增长，我也越来越注意防晒了，所以这是个很棒的建议。这是某个品牌推荐的吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah. So Beauty of Joseon is the brand.
turns.zh: 是的。Joseon Beauty这个品牌。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beauty of Joseon.
turns.zh: Joseon Beauty。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: There's another brand, Isntree, which also has a great sunscreen. But I'll be honest, almost every Korean sunscreen I've tried is great.
turns.zh: 还有Isntree这个品牌，他们的防晒霜也很棒。不过说实话，我试过的几乎所有韩国防晒霜都很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I'm Googling this as soon as we get off. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to and share and or share with family and friends even more [inaudible 01:11:39]?
turns.zh: 好的。一结束我就去搜一下。你有没有最喜欢的座右铭，经常回想、分享给家人朋友的？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: I do. So there's a John Steinbeck quote, which I'm not big on quotes, but I like this one, which is that, "It's a common experience that a problem difficult at night is resolved in the morning after the committee of sleep has worked on it." I find that that's something I really live by. First off, I love sleep and I try to get as much of it as possible. But the other thing is that if I'm stuck on a problem or if I am writing a response to something like a tense issue or an emotional issue, often I find that if I put down my thoughts, go to sleep, check it in the morning, I end up with a better outcome. So all of a sudden you have a new perspective and clarity on a problem you were stuck on, or you realize that you weren't clear in the way you were communicating your thoughts because you were emotional about something and you're able to put together a much better response to an e-mail or to whatever problem you're handling. So sleep can solve lots of problems.
turns.zh: 是的，我确实认同这一点。这里有一句约翰·斯坦贝克的名言，虽然我不太喜欢引用名言，但我很喜欢这句：“夜晚难以解决的问题，到了清晨，在睡眠委员会工作过后，往往就能迎刃而解。” 我发现这句话确实是我生活中的真谛。首先，我热爱睡眠，尽可能多睡。但另一方面，如果我被某个问题困住，或者在回复敏感或情绪化议题时卡壳，往往放下思绪入睡，次日清晨再重新审视时，就能得到更好的解决方案。比如，你会突然对困住你的问题产生新的视角和清晰的思路，或者意识到自己因情绪激动而未能清晰传达想法，从而能更好地回复邮件或处理手头难题。可见睡眠能解决许多问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love sleep as well. I'm always telling my wife, "Let's go to sleep." Like, "Okay, I'll be there soon." I love that advice. Okay, two more questions. Who's influenced you most in your career? Is there someone that comes to mind?
turns.zh: 我也喜欢睡眠。我总是对我妻子说：“咱们睡吧。”比如，“好的，我马上就到。” 我很喜欢这种建议。好的，再问两个问题。谁对你的职业生涯影响最大？你能想到谁吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: So I think two answers, a multi-part answer. So I think first my career has been in male-dominated industries and I've worked with just some incredible women who've really influenced me. When I was a banker, there were two senior bankers, Vanessa Roberts and Gina Tarone at Lehman Brothers where I worked. And they were just so incredible. They were just so good at their jobs and I found that really inspiring. (01:13:29): And then at DoorDash, Tia Sherringham, who is our GC, and Liz Jarvis-Shean, who leads comms, are just dominant in their fields. And I think that that's really empowering and have been big influences on me to just see strong, powerful women kicking ass and that helps me believe that I can do the same. So that's one answer. (01:13:54): And then the other answer, sort of cliche, but my parents. My mom was a statistician at the UN before she got married, and she actually chose to stay home and raise three children, so I'm the youngest. And when I was in, I think it was elementary school, decided to go back to school, switch careers and become a nurse. And so the fact that she embarked on this completely new career in her forties after 15 years as a stay-at-home mom and my father supported this. I think that that was really, really influential and was probably the first time I saw that you can do whatever you put your mind to, no matter your age, no matter your circumstances. So that was really influential and I don't think I've ever told her that. So hi, Mom.
turns.zh: 我觉得有两个答案，一个多部分的回答。首先，我的职业生涯一直在男性主导的行业中工作，但遇到过一些非常出色的女性，她们真正影响了我。比如，我做银行家时，雷曼兄弟公司的两位资深银行家——凡妮莎·罗伯茨和吉娜·塔罗内，她们太了不起了。她们在工作中表现出色，我深受启发。（01:13:29）：然后在DoorDash，首席法务官蒂娅·谢林汉姆和负责公关的利兹·贾维斯-希恩，在各自领域都非常出色。我认为这真的很鼓舞人心，能看到强大的女性在事业上大放异彩，这让我相信自己也能做到。（01:13:54）：再说另一个答案，可能有些老生常谈，但就是我的父母。我母亲在结婚前曾是联合国统计员，但后来选择留在家中抚养三个孩子，我是最小的。我记得自己上小学时，决定重返校园，转行成为护士。她四十多岁，在做了15年全职妈妈后，开始这份全新的职业，而我父亲全力支持她。我认为这真的很有影响力，这可能是我第一次意识到，无论年龄多大，无论身处何种境遇，只要下定决心，就能达成目标。这对我影响很大，但我从未对她说过。所以，妈妈，您好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hi Mom. Thank you, mom.
turns.zh: 妈妈，你好。谢谢你，妈妈。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, I think that was influential for my career. Definitely.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这对我的职业生涯很有影响。绝对的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a beautiful answer. Fun fact, I worked with Liz at Airbnb. Your person you just mentioned in the comms team.
turns.zh: 这真是个精彩的回答。趣闻是，我在Airbnb时和利兹共事过。你刚刚提到的公关团队里的那位。

turns.en: She's amazing. Final question. So when you joined DoorDash, imagine it wasn't obvious that it was going to work. I imagine it was still like, "This was a crazy idea. Maybe it'll work, maybe not." Is there a moment you recall where you're like, "I think this is going to be a big success? I think this is actually going to work out?"
turns.zh: 她太了不起了。最后一个问题。那么当你加入DoorDash时，想象一下当时并没有明显的迹象表明它会成功。我想当时大家可能还在想：“这真是个疯狂的想法。也许它能成功，也许不行。”你是否记得有那么一个时刻，你突然觉得：“我觉得这会大获成功！我觉得这事儿肯定能成！”

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: To be honest, I went into DoorDash because I wanted to learn for the experience. I thought it was interesting, problems with interesting people. I never thought too much about whether it would work. I of course wanted it to work and was very competitive and wanted to win. I think there's two moments that stand out. One was when the third party market share data showed that we had become the number one player after, I think we started at number four or five. And I think that that was really exciting to see the trajectory and to see us gain in category share. That was exciting. I probably didn't see it until months after it had happened because we don't spend a ton of time focusing on it, but I do remember somebody wanted to include the graph in some presentation, some sales material, and we're like, "Oh, we're number one. That's incredible. We used to be number five." So I'd say that that was one. (01:16:17): The other one that stands out was, the first talk I gave in a lot of these startup talks in the early days in Boston, and I'd asked the audience, "How many of you have used DoorDash?" And there'd be like three people who would raise their hand. And then it was a few years ago, maybe 2018, 2019, and I was giving a talk and I asked the audience, "How many of you have used DoorDash?" And almost everyone's hands went up. And that was actually pretty memorable for me because in my mind, we were still the small startup that no one had heard of where I had to over enunciate the D's in DoorDash. So people didn't think I worked for Jordash, the nineties' denim company. And so that was pretty meaningful to me when just so many people had used the product or were consumers of DoorDash. It was pretty exciting. And I still get excited. I saw DoorDash mentioned in a book recently that I was reading. It was like, "We're in the book." So those little things when you become part of the cultural lingo that I think are really, really special.
turns.zh: 说实话，我加入DoorDash是因为我想从中学习经验。我觉得这很有趣，是和有趣的人一起解决问题。当时我并没太想它能否成功。我当然希望它能成功，我很有竞争意识，渴望赢得胜利。我觉得有两个时刻特别值得回味。一个是第三方市场份额数据显示，我们从最初的四五名一跃成为第一名的时候。我觉得看到这个趋势，看到我们在品类份额上不断提升，真是太激动了。这事儿直到几个月后我才意识到，因为我们平时不怎么关注这些数据，但我记得有人想把图表放进演示文稿或销售材料里，我们当时就说：“哇，我们是第一名了。太不可思议了。我们以前可是第五名啊。”所以我觉得这算一个时刻。（01:16:17）另一个时刻是在波士顿早期创业活动上，我第一次做演讲时，问听众：“有多少人用过DoorDash？”当时只有三个人举手。几年前，大概2018年或2019年，再做演讲时，我问听众：“有多少人用过DoorDash？”几乎所有人都举手了。这对我来说意义非凡，因为在我看来，我们当时还是个默默无闻的小创业公司，我甚至得把DoorDash的D发音强调清楚，免得人们以为我在为90年代的牛仔裤品牌Jordash工作。所以当那么多人用过DoorDash，或者是DoorDash的消费者时，我真的很感动。这太令人兴奋了。直到最近，我还在读的一本书里看到提到了DoorDash。书里写道：“我们上书了。”所以这些小细节，当你成为文化语境的一部分时，真的非常特别。

Go team DoorDash. (01:17:44): Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to follow stuff that you do? I know you've been doing more writing on LinkedIn and things like that, so just help people understand where to find you and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 嗯，我是DoorDash的忠实用户。从来没有过“永不送达”的情况。虽然有时送货会晚一点，但通常都很完美。感谢你们所做的一切。DoorDash团队加油。（01:17:44）最后两个问题。如果大家想关注你的动态，哪里可以找到你？我知道你最近在LinkedIn上写了不少文章之类的，能帮大家了解一下如何找到你吗？

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yeah, so as you mentioned, to find me LinkedIn, I don't have a huge social presence, but I am on LinkedIn and I am currently writing a series of blog posts about my experience building a global analytics org at DoorDash. Some of the lessons I've learned over the last 10 years. So definitely check those out. (01:18:16): And as far as your second question of how listeners can be useful to me, I guess read the post on LinkedIn and I'd love to hear what people think, whether you agree with my point of view or not. That being said, be nice. I want honest feedback, but I want kindness as well. So yeah, just engage with the content and let me know what y'all think. I think I do have a broader ask, which is just to encourage folks listening to TruthSeek, something I take seriously at DoorDash. It's a company value. But there's a lot of misinformation out there and it's often up to us as individuals to figure out what's fact and what's fiction. So I have a plea for folks to do your best, to search for the truth and speak the truth, and I think we'll all be better off for it. And of course, use DoorDash.
turns.zh: 是的，正如你提到的，想在领英上找到我，我在社交媒体上的活跃度不算高，但我确实有领英账号，目前正在写一系列博客文章，分享我在DoorDash建立全球分析部门的经验，分享过去10年里我学到的一些教训。所以一定要去看看那些内容。（01:18:16）至于你提到的第二个问题，听众如何能对我有所帮助，我想说，去读我在领英上的那篇帖子，我很期待听到大家的想法，无论你们是否认同我的观点。不过请保持友善。我希望得到诚实的反馈，同时也希望大家能友善相待。所以请积极参与内容讨论，让我知道你们的想法。我确实还有一个更宏大的请求，那就是鼓励听众们关注《TruthSeek》节目。这是我在DoorDash非常重视的一项价值观。但现在网上有很多虚假信息，往往需要我们每个人去辨别真假。所以我恳请大家尽力搜寻真相、说出真相，我相信这样对我们大家都有好处。当然，也欢迎大家使用DoorDash。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Of course.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Jessica Lachs
turns.en: Yes, there are three things that listeners can do.
turns.zh: 是的，听众可以做三件事。

turns.en: You're at DoorDash.com. That was awesome. I love that last point as well in addition, to use DoorDash. Jessica, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 你可以在DoorDash.com上找到我。太棒了。我也很喜欢最后一点——使用DoorDash。杰西卡，非常感谢你能来。
